2: Why does this gate need code?
Because revocation is where card sign-in quietly breaks.
If an issuing certificate authority in the trust store has no revocation list configured, Entra doesn't check revocation for that authority's certificates at all.
If a list is configured but can't be downloaded in time, certificate-based authentication fails for every card from that authority.
And a revocation list grows with every revocation, so a list that fits today can cross your cloud's limit next month.
None of those shows up in a one-time configuration review.
So this module measures each list and checks the tenant's settings against your cloud's limits, every day rather than once.

5: Here are the limits the check holds each cloud to.
G C C uses the commercial service, so its interactive sign-in limit for a revocation list is twenty megabytes.
G C C High is Azure Government, at forty-five megabytes, and the kit holds D O D to the same.
In every cloud a list must download within ten seconds.
Learn gives those limits in megabytes; the kit reads them as decimal megabytes, a million bytes each, which is the stricter reading.
There's no default cloud in the kit: you name it every time, so a G C C High check can't silently run against G C C's numbers.
Two thresholds are the program's design guidance, not Learn's: a warning at eighty percent of the interactive limit, and a warning when an authority's certificate expires within ninety days.
6: Unit 2 has two parts, the measurement and the check.
The measurement downloads each revocation list once and records its size in bytes, the seconds it took and any error, with the time it was measured.
An unreachable list isn't an exception that stops the run: it's recorded, because the failure is exactly the finding you want.
For the lab, a local path is read as a file, which is how Lab 1 runs on a laptop with no network.
In Lab 2 you measure the real lists from outside the agency network.
And the check insists on the measurement.
A configured list with no measurement row is C B six, a Finding, so you can't pass the check by skipping the download.
7: The check runs thirteen rules, C B one to C B thirteen.
Eight of them look at the trust store and the lists.
C B twelve: an issuing authority the card program uses isn't in the trust store.
C B one: an authority has no revocation list configured, so Entra doesn't check revocation for it.
A root with no list is only a warning to confirm, since a root that issues only authority certificates may publish none.
C B two: the list's endpoint isn't plain H T T P, which Learn recommends.
C B four: the list couldn't be downloaded, or took longer than ten seconds.
C B three: the list is over the cloud's interactive limit.
C B five warns at eighty percent of it.
And C B eleven warns when an authority's certificate expires within ninety days.
8: The other five rules look at the method and the policy.
C B seven: the X dot five-oh-nine certificate method isn't enabled.
C B eight warns when revocation list validation isn't required of every authority, or when an authority is exempted from it.
An exemption is allowed only while that authority's list is being fixed, and with an end date.
C B nine: a piv policy O I D isn't mapped to multifactor, and the default mode is single-factor, so a card sign-in may not count as multifactor.
C B thirteen warns about low-affinity username bindings.
And C B ten is the scuba rule: no enabled Conditional Access policy for all users and all resources requires a phishing-resistant strength.
A strength counts only if every combination it allows is fido two, Windows Hello for Business, or multifactor certificate.

10: Step three checks the fictional tenant for G C C.
The first line names the limits it's using: twenty million bytes, and ten seconds.
Then the count: five Findings, seven Warns, and exit code two.
The lab asks you to find four of them.
C B four: one authority's list took eleven point four seconds to download, over the ten-second limit, so in real life sign-in would fail for its cards.
C B five: that same list is eighteen and a half million bytes, more than eighty percent of the G C C limit.
C B nine: the piv policy O I D isn't mapped to multifactor.

11: Step four runs the same check on the same tenant, naming G C C High instead.
The limit line now says forty-five million bytes, and the count drops to five Findings and six Warns.
One warning went away: C B five.
The eighteen and a half million byte list was over eighty percent of G C C's twenty megabytes, but it's well under eighty percent of forty-five, so in G C C High it's fine.
The ten-second limit applies in every cloud, so the eleven point four second download is still a Finding.
That's the lesson of this step: the same list can be a warning in one cloud and not in another, which is why the check always takes the cloud by name.
